title: Estimate, Then Count
subject: math
learningGoal: Make a sensible estimate and check it by counting in groups.
realWorldHook: Shopkeepers and cooks estimate all the time: 'about how many will we need?'

materials.item: A cup of something countable (dry pasta, buttons)
materials.householdSubstitution: Socks in a basket, toy blocks, or crayons

noPurchaseRoute: Use any pile of 20 to 60 things you already have, like socks, blocks or crayons.
parentPreview: Your child looks at a pile, makes an estimate, then counts by grouping into tens. Comparing the estimate with the count is the learning: close is great.

parent.parentSays: Look at this pile but don't count. About how many do you think there are?
parent.whyThisWorks: An estimate is a thoughtful guess. Writing it down makes the later count exciting.

child.screen: Don't count yet! How many do you think?
child.readAloudText: Don't count yet. How many do you think there are?

parent.parentSays: Now let's count by making little piles of ten.
parent.whyThisWorks: Grouping into tens is faster, easier to check, and builds place value.

parent.parentSays: How many piles of ten? How many left over? So how many altogether?
Was your estimate close? Would you guess higher or lower next time?

child.readAloudText: Was your guess close, too high or too low?

parent.parentSays: Ask the two check questions below. Give your child time to think, then note how each one went.
Where would estimating be useful at home?

expectedResponses: An estimate within about 10 of the count

misconceptions.signal: Guesses a very large or random number without looking.
misconceptions.supportiveNextQuestion: If there were 100, would the pile be bigger or smaller than this?

misconceptions.signal: Recounts from the start or double-counts items.
misconceptions.supportiveNextQuestion: How could piles of ten help us not lose our place?

checkQuestions.parentAsks: 3 piles of ten and 4 left over. How many?

interpretation.partial: Counts on from 30 or counts all.

child.screen: 3 piles of ten and 4 left over. How many?
child.readAloudText: Three piles of ten and four left over. How many altogether?

checkQuestions.parentAsks: About how many people could sit in our living room? Is 5, 50 or 500 most sensible?

interpretation.clear: Chooses a sensible size and explains.

child.screen: How many people could fit in your living room?
child.readAloudText: How many people could sit in your living room? About five, fifty or five hundred?

extension: Estimate a bigger pile (100+). Use piles of ten and then groups of ten piles.

shorterVersion.description: Estimate and count one small pile.

accessibilityAdaptations: Use larger objects that are easier to pick up.
Use an egg carton or cups to hold the groups of ten.
